html:
A complete message to hear and restate

Adult or partner models this whole message in the learner’s communication mode: “Our paper bridge needs a wide base. That will help it stand. Then we can add the road.” A possible restatement is “The wide base comes first so the bridge can stand.” A connected addition is “Could we add supports beside the base?” Rephrase rather than demand exact repetition.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
One sentence in two occasions

Sentence: “Could we compare the two designs?” Occasion A: two familiar partners are choosing a bridge. Occasion B: a chaired school meeting; the chair invites a student question. Model the same clear sentence in both contexts, attending to the agreed turn. Discuss how the wording can suit both and how the occasion changes when a turn is taken. Pace and comfortable volume support communication; they are not separate performance targets here.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Source-backed roles and checked host guidance

Reconciliation Australia explains that a Welcome to Country is delivered by Traditional Owners, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people given permission by Traditional Owners. Anyone can offer an Acknowledgement of Country. The roles and purposes differ; arrangements and appropriate wording depend on context. Consult local representative bodies and the actual hosts when planning an event.

For a real visit, ask the host how to participate and when to ask questions. The fictional host directions used in this lesson are supplied for that scenario only. Do not turn them into rules for every First Nations community, invent local language or imitate a ceremony.

Read Reconciliation Australia’s explanation of Welcome and Acknowledgement roles
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Display discussion · another round

The group has three paper models: a boat, a bridge and a bird. Proposed plan: all models go on a low table; labels go beside their objects; a wide gap stays clear for visitors. Eva says, “Let’s put the bridge in the middle so people can see both sides.”

Restate Eva’s idea, add a connected suggestion, ask a useful question and negotiate moving on to the display title.

For example: “You want the bridge in the middle so both sides can be seen. Could the boat go at one end? How much space should we leave? When we have agreed on places, could we choose the title?” Accept equivalent relevant language and a real chance for others to reply. Check the group’s final plan by asking what each person will do.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · clarify a whole message

The group has agreed to let each person finish. Alex says, “Put the large label above the boat and the small label beside the bird.” You heard the boat instruction but missed where the small label belongs.

Give a suitable next response and a way to check the plan.

Wait for Alex to finish, then ask a relevant clarification such as “Where should the small label go?” A check could restate “Large label above the boat; small label beside the bird—is that right?” Accept equivalent wording that checks the actual missing information.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · choose the convention

In pair work, your partner has just finished an idea. At a separate class meeting, the chair has asked everyone to wait for an invitation before asking questions.

Explain how you could ask a question in each setting. Must you use longer words in the meeting?

In the pair, ask after the partner finishes. In the meeting, use its agreed invitation process, then ask clearly. The words may be the same, such as “Could you explain that part?” Longer words are not required. The conventions, roles and context explain the difference.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · specific feedback

Maya says, “Let’s write our display title on the smallest card.” The display will be read from across the classroom. A larger blank card is available.

Give useful feedback and a suggestion, then check whether Maya agrees.

For example: “The title tells visitors our topic, but the small card may be hard to read from across the room. Could we use the larger card? What do you think?” It names a relevant issue and improvement while leaving space for a response. Other clear, respectful versions are valid.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
The complete warning story behind the opinion

“Keep the lid shut or the paper stars will blow away,” said the keeper. Dara nodded and put the lid down. A gust shook the table. “Keep the lid shut,” the keeper warned again. Dara reached for the ribbon, the lid lifted, and the stars scattered across the floor. Dara and the keeper gathered every star and tied the lid down.

A reader can support “I found the ending effective because the repeated warning built suspense” by naming the repeated warning and the later scattering. That is one supported judgement, not a response everyone must share.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A complete record and a judgement

Prepared fictional record: “The new playground opened on Monday. It has two swings.” Response: “The brilliant new playground is exciting.” The record supplies checkable model facts; brilliant and exciting add evaluation or feeling. Explain whose judgement is being expressed rather than claiming every reader must feel excited.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Revision card 1 · an offered choice

A group leader wants to offer drawing as one possible quiet activity. The draft says, “You must draw while we wait.”

Replace the modal so it offers the activity as a choice, and explain the effect.

“You could draw while we wait” offers a possibility or suggestion instead of a requirement. Other clear choice wording, such as “You can choose to draw”, can work; explain how it fits the stated purpose.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Revision card 2 · a narrator’s impression

Version A: “The rabbit pushed past the other animals.” Version B: “The rabbit politely waited for the other animals.” These fictional versions deliberately give different actions and attitudes.

Name a verb and an adverb that create the different evaluations. Does changing A into B preserve all facts?

Pushed contrasts with waited, and politely presents an approving attitude in B. The action has changed as well as the impression, so the versions do not preserve all facts. A writer may choose either for a different fictional character portrayal.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Revision card 3 · stronger pleasure

“At last, the repaired kite flew. Sol felt pleased with the result.” The writer wants stronger pleasure, not anger or fear.

Replace pleased and explain why your word fits the intended feeling.

Delighted is one suitable choice: it expresses stronger pleasure in this context. Thrilled may also work. Terrified would change the emotion to fear, and furious would change it to anger.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · probability and obligation

A rule says, “Visitors must stay behind the line.” A prediction says, “The bus could arrive early.”

Explain the modal’s job in each sentence. Rewrite the prediction to sound more certain without turning it into a rule.

Must expresses a requirement to stay behind the line. Could expresses a possible arrival. “The bus will arrive early” sounds more certain as a prediction; it is still the speaker’s claim rather than proof of the future.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · noun, verb and adverb choices

Fictional narrator A: “The helper gently guided the lost cub.” Narrator B: “The troublemaker roughly shoved the lost cub.”

Compare one noun, one verb and one adverb and explain the impressions. Are these merely different spellings of the same facts?

Helper/troublemaker gives approving/disapproving labels; guided/shoved changes the action and force; gently/roughly changes manner. The versions present meaningfully different behaviour and evaluations, so they are not fact-preserving swaps. Discuss fictional actions rather than fixed labels for classmates.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · supported judgement

“Uma saw that the display sign had fallen. She set it upright so visitors could read it. Then she returned to her own work.”

Give a supported judgement of Uma’s action and a reason. Then express mild or strong pleasure in your own response and name which you chose.

Helpful or thoughtful is supported by setting the sign upright for visitors. For example, “I was pleased that Uma helped” expresses pleasure; “I was delighted that Uma helped” expresses stronger pleasure in this comparison. Accept another accurate judgement or response with evidence; do not infer an exact hidden feeling for Uma.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete extra structure models

Procedure, “Make a paper name card”: “Materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil. First, fold the paper in half. Next, write the model’s name on the front. Finally, stand the folded card beside the model.” The sequence tells the reader what to do.

Information report, “Our name cards”: “Materials: Each card is paper. Shape: Each folded card stands like a small tent. Use: A card names the model beside it.” Grouped facts help the reader find materials, shape or use.

Narrative, “The missing card”: “Jo placed a card beside the model boat. A breeze blew the card under the table. Jo found it and put a small weight on it. The visitors could read the boat’s name.” The linked events introduce and resolve a problem.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete mixed-up recount for the retained transfer task

Sentence cards: A “Finally, we put the labelled models on the table.” B “On Thursday, our class prepared a display.” C “First, we made the models; then we wrote their labels.”

Arrange the three cards into a clear recount and explain one organising change.

B, C, A gives the occasion before the ordered events and ending. The time words and the need to make and label models before displaying them support that order. The repair helps a reader follow what happened; it is more than changing a pronoun.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh comparison · recount and autobiographical model

Class reporter’s factual recount: “On Monday, our class measured the display tables. First, the teacher gave each group a ruler. Next, the groups recorded the lengths. Finally, the class compared the records.” Fictional autobiographical model written in invented character Dev’s voice: “I first enjoyed measuring when I helped make a toy house. I measured its walls with my aunt. Later, I started keeping drawings of my designs. I still like finding out how things fit.”

Compare purpose, viewpoint and one organising choice in the two complete texts.

The factual recount records a particular class event in time order, using first/next/finally. Dev’s model selects experiences from the character’s own life in I/my voice and ends with a personal reflection. Both use past experiences. The autobiographical model is explicitly fictional; I alone is not proof that a text is a true autobiography.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh comparison · report and explanation

Report, “Our balancing model”: “Parts: A card strip rests on a block. A small toy sits on each end. Position: The block is under the middle of the strip.” Explanation, “How this model tips”: “At first, the strip rests level on the block. When we move one toy farther from the middle, that end of this prepared model goes down. The changed toy position makes this model tip.”

Which text groups parts and position, and which follows a change and its result? Explain how the arrangement serves each purpose.

The report groups facts under Parts and Position so a reader can find a property of the model. The explanation connects the changed position to the observed tipping result in this prepared model. It explains how the change occurs rather than listing parts. No calculation or general physics rule is required.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh comparison · story, verse and response

Narrative, “The loose wheel”: “In art time, Lin’s paper cart lost a wheel. Lin could not make it stand. Ari held the cart while Lin fixed the wheel. The cart rolled across the desk, and both children cheered.” Verse, “Paper cart”: “Wobble, little paper wheel; / wait beside the line. / Steady hands can help you stand; / now your turn to shine.” Personal response: “I liked The loose wheel because Ari’s small act of holding the cart makes the repair possible.”

Describe one organisation or language choice in each text and connect it to its purpose.

The story links a problem, help and resolution to entertain through events. The verse uses four lines, repeated sounds or imagined address to a wheel, creating a playful focus rather than merely listing facts. The response gives a view and a story-based reason. Accept other accurate feature-effect links; do not require everyone to like the story.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh comparison · argument and information

Argument: “We should keep a ruler beside the display table. First, makers could check whether a model fits the space. Second, visitors could measure a model if the teacher invites them to. Let’s keep one ruler in a labelled place.” Information: “The class ruler is 30 centimetres long. It is kept beside the display table. Its marks show centimetres.”

Identify the four argument stages and compare the main purposes of the texts. Why would “The ruler is yellow” be a weak extra reason for this proposal?

The argument introduces a proposal, gives a fit-checking reason, gives a visitor-measuring reason, and concludes with an action request. It aims to persuade; the other text informs about the ruler. Colour is merely related information unless a further relevant reason is explained. It does not by itself support keeping a ruler there.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.
Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete mixed-up text for the retained transfer task

Draft: “Our seed pots have name labels. The labels stand beside each plant. Our tools hang by the door. Large writing makes the labels easy to read. A watering can stands under the tools.”

Choose a useful paragraph break or move, make it, and explain how it helps.

One repair groups the first, second and fourth sentences as labels, then groups the third and fifth as tools: “Our seed pots have name labels. The labels stand beside each plant. Large writing makes the labels easy to read.” New paragraph: “Our tools hang by the door. A watering can stands under the tools.” The related information stays together; no facts need to be removed.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · group and open two paragraphs

Sentence cards: A “A tray catches loose paper.” B “Our art shelf keeps materials in groups.” C “A pot holds the pencils.” D “Our display table gives models space.” E “Wide gaps separate the models.” F “A clear edge keeps the route open.”

Make two paragraphs, choose their openings and explain why the details belong together.

One arrangement is B, C, A for grouped art materials, and D, E, F for the display’s space and route. B and D introduce the corresponding topics. A/C can swap without harming the meaning. Either whole-paragraph order is acceptable when justified; do not impose an arbitrary order.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · repair mixed groups

Draft: “Our tool box is easy to carry. It has two strong handles. Our signs use large writing. Each sign names a display. A light lid covers the box.”

Repair the paragraph grouping while keeping all the useful information.

For example: “Our tool box is easy to carry. It has two strong handles. A light lid covers the box.” New paragraph: “Our signs use large writing. Each sign names a display.” The box details and sign details now stay in useful groups. The box is introduced before It; all supplied information is retained.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · narrative breaks

Paragraph 1: “Before school, Bea placed a paper boat on the window ledge. She left to fetch its label.” Paragraph 2: “When she came back, the boat had vanished.” Paragraph 3: “Bea looked down. The boat lay on the floor below the open window. She picked it up and closed the window.”

Explain one reason for the first break and one possible effect of the short middle paragraph.

The first break marks a time change and introduces the missing-boat problem. The short middle paragraph gives that problem emphasis before the next paragraph develops the search and recovery. It does not need the same topic-and-support pattern as an informative paragraph.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.
Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

Draft page heading: “Garden guide”. Its section labelled “More” contains “Trowels belong on the lower shelf. Watering cans belong beside the door.” Another section labelled “Visiting” contains the opening time and gate information.

Improve the vague section label and give a useful subheading for each tool. Explain how the changes guide a reader.

Tool storage is a useful replacement for More. Subheadings Trowels and Watering cans separate the tool facts. The labels predict the actual information so readers can choose a specific route. Retain the supplied storage facts and use the working local links for actual digital navigation.

html:
Fresh check · print hierarchy

Use the prepared Class garden guide in this section. Its contents sends Visiting to page 4 and Tool storage to page 6. Page 4 has Opening times and Where to enter; page 6 has Trowels and Watering cans.

Find when the garden opens and where watering cans belong. Name the page route and most specific subheading for each.

Visiting → page 4 → Opening times gives after the morning bell. Tool storage → page 6 → Watering cans gives beside the door. A broad section is a route, while the subheading narrows the search; the actual sentence confirms the answer.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · digital confirmation

Use the actual working garden and tool menus in this section. The tasks are to find the entry gate and where trowels belong.

Follow both useful links, check their headings and information, then return to each menu. Explain one reason the link words help.

Where to enter reaches the shed-gate information; Trowel storage reaches the lower-shelf information. Return links reach the corresponding menus. The link words name the information need. Observe actual use of the links for digital navigation; a spoken route description alone is only planning evidence.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Fresh check · a complete chapter-title comparison

Prepared narrative contents: Chapter 1 “The locked drawer”, page 2; Chapter 2 “A key by the paint pot”, page 5. Chapter 2 text: “Ari moved the empty paint pot. A small key lay underneath it. Ari tried the key in the drawer, and the lock opened.”

Which chapter title suggests where to look for the key event? Check what the actual text says: was the key inside the pot?

Chapter 2 points to the key event. The supplied text says the key was underneath the pot, not inside it. The title suggests the event and creates interest, but the detailed text is needed to check location. A chapter title need not provide a precise complete account of every event.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete clause cards

  1. The small rabbit is quiet.
  2. The rabbits beside the pond are quiet.
  3. The basket of leaves rest by the door.
  4. Mina and Jo carries the basket.
  5. While the wind blew, the children were reading indoors.

Mark each whole subject and verb group. Repair cards 3 and 4. Then join “The dog slept” and “The children painted” with while. Say which clause needs the rest of the resulting sentence.

Check and explain

1: The small rabbit / is. 2: The rabbits beside the pond / are. 3: The basket of leaves / rests. 4: Mina and Jo / carry. 5: the wind / blew; the children / were reading. One joined version is “While the dog slept, the children painted.” The while part depends on its partner here. A valid alternative is “The dog slept while the children painted”; identify the while clause in the actual version.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Answers for the earlier grammar comparisons

In “Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet”, small describes the shorebirds, quickly describes their manner of flying, and across the inlet adds location. The whole subject is Small shorebirds; fly is the verb. “We stayed inside because it rained” contains we / stayed and it / rained. The because part gives the reason. “It rained, so we stayed inside” presents the rain first and makes the result explicit. Formal clause labels are not required.

In “The dog chased the ball”, the dog is the subject and chased is the verb. In “The ball was chased by the dog”, the ball is the subject and was chased is the whole verb group. The subject is not always the doer. These forms retain the same chasing event; this is a supported comparison, not a requirement to master passive forms.

Fresh transfer: change “The dog near the trees runs” so it names two dogs. One answer is “The dogs near the trees run”. Changing the subject number requires changing this present verb too.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A concrete quick correction

“The box of pens are full” names one box; write is full. Pointing only to pens misses the main subject word. In “The box is full”, is is already a verb. A correct explanation names the subject and the matching form.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh clause and agreement check

Read: “While the bell rang, the children was packing. The bag of books rest by the door.” Find the subject–verb pairs, then repair the two agreement errors. Keep the first sentence in the past and the second in the present.

Check and explain

The bell / rang; the children / were packing; The bag of books / rests. Change was to were for children, and rest to rests for one bag. Keep were packing together. The while clause needs its partner in this sentence.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A complete story with all five verb meanings

“Fen opened the box. ‘Here it is,’ Fen said. Fen remembered the missing key and loved its shiny ribbon. The key had a round handle.”

Find opened, said, remembered, loved and had. Explain the different information each gives. Is in the quoted speech also relates it to here in this context.

Check and explain

Opened: doing, an action with the box. Said: saying, a spoken message. Remembered: thinking, a memory. Loved: feeling about its ribbon. Had: relating, a feature possessed by the key. These are different kinds of meaning in these exact clauses.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Use the earlier evaluation examples to inspect verbs

The earlier examples also contain verbs. In “I liked the story”, liked expresses a feeling. In “The playground opened on Monday”, opened presents an event. In “The playground is exciting”, is relates the playground to a description. The words brilliant and exciting evaluate the playground but are not whole verb groups in that description.

Complete fresh comparison: “Jo whispered, ‘The gate is open.’” Change whispered to shouted. Both are saying verbs. Shouted changes the indicated delivery; it does not establish Jo’s reason or feeling. For the earlier stronger/weaker judgement task, compare “I liked the ending” and “I loved the ending”. Both express a positive feeling, with loved usually stronger in this context. Accept a supported explanation of a different intended feeling.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A concrete quick correction

In “Fen remembered the key”, remembered is a verb even though it does not name visible movement. In “The key has a round handle”, has relates a feature to the key. Naming the verb is a start; explain the particular information it gives.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh five-meaning check

“Sam carried the tray. ‘It is heavy,’ Sam said. Sam remembered the spilled water and disliked the slippery floor. The tray had two handles.” Find a verb for doing, saying, thinking, feeling and relating. Explain the information each gives.

Check and explain

Carried: doing, the movement of the tray. Said: saying, the spoken comment. Remembered: thinking, a memory. Disliked: feeling about the floor. Had: relating, possession of handles. Is also relates it to heavy. Accept either clear relating example. Use meanings in the actual clauses.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete time cards

  1. Habit: Each morning Jo ___ the plants. Use water.
  2. Completed yesterday: Jo ___ the plants and ___ home. Use water and go.
  3. Plan for tomorrow: Jo will ___ the plants. Use water.
  4. Recount to repair: Yesterday we made a sign. We put it by the bed and carry the tools home.

Choose the forms and explain the time. Finally write a new garden message with one past event, one present habit and one future plan.

Check and explain

1: waters, a present habit. 2: watered and went, past events. 3: water, the base form after will. 4: change carry to carried. Made and put already fit the past recount. An original message might be “Yesterday we planted beans. We water them each morning. Tomorrow we will check the soil.” Accept other clear messages with matching forms and explicit intended time changes.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Apply time changes to the earlier examples

“Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet” uses fly; to describe one completed event yesterday, write “Small shorebirds flew quickly across the inlet yesterday”. Flew is the past form of fly. The added describing words do not create the tense change.

“We stayed inside because it rained” and “It rained, so we stayed inside” both use past verbs, stayed and rained. Their different ordering shows the reason/result relationship, not a change in time. “The dog chased the ball” and “The ball was chased by the dog” both describe the past chasing event. Was chased is the whole group in the second form; formal passive terminology is not required.

Fresh transfer: change “The children carry the box” into a completed event yesterday and a plan for tomorrow. Answers: “Yesterday the children carried the box” and “Tomorrow the children will carry the box”. Explain carried and will carry.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A concrete quick correction

In “Yesterday Jo took a cup”, took supplies past form and yesterday makes the time explicit. Do not replace took with taked. An explanation should name both the form and intended time rather than saying it sounds better.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh time check

This message has two yesterday events and one tomorrow plan: “Yesterday Jo caught a ball. Jo carry it home. Tomorrow Jo will play again.” Repair the middle verb, identify the whole future group and explain why one time change stays.

Check and explain

Use carried. Caught and carried describe yesterday’s events; will play is the whole future group. The tomorrow plan is a justified change of time. “Will plays” would not fit this construction.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Actual images for the earlier visual tasks

The meeting drawing adds facing direction, distance, expression and a shared object. The viewer comparison changes framing and gaze while keeping its words the same. These are drawings, not photographs. For the earlier transfer task, use the different gate try below rather than an unseen picture.

Check and explain

The gate try shows widely spaced figures facing away, folded arms and straight mouths. These details may suggest distance or disagreement. The written caption alone supplies only waiting. The reason and earlier events remain unknown.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A useful labelled diagram

Use the preserved picnic-area map in Worked example and reasoning checks. The labels identify the picnic area, creek and bridge; the dotted line shows a walking route to the bridge. That image supplies route information beyond “The picnic area is beside the creek”. Layout can help us locate a label; the route itself supplies the added meaning.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A concrete quick correction

In the meeting drawing, the shared box and facing figures may suggest cooperation. “They have been best friends for years” goes beyond the evidence. A close face may invite attention, but viewers do not all have to feel the same emotion.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
A fresh visual version to create

Use this new caption: “The friends found the box.” Draw two figures far apart, one facing the other and offering the box. Add a second version with the figures close together, both reaching for it. Explain a visible difference and a possible difference in relationship. Name something the words and images leave unknown.

Check and explain

Check the actual drawing: the caption stays the same and the specified position or gesture changes are visible. For example, an offered box may suggest an invitation, while both reaching could suggest sharing or competing, depending on the drawn expressions. Accept supported possibilities; the drawings do not prove ownership or earlier events.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html: The actual arrival illustration for the earlier try
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete vocabulary cards

  1. Measurement record: a card is 9 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide; its edge strip is 3 millimetres wide. Report the card’s length and the strip’s width using number and unit.
  2. Story: “At noon beside the pond, a duck named Dot lost a feather. A frog found it and Dot put it in a nest.” Use character, setting and plot to describe this story.
  3. Two senses: “The feather is light. It weighs almost nothing.” “We need light to see the nest.” Explain light in each sentence, using a nearby clue.
  4. Word family: “The first drawing was unclear. I will draw it again.” Replace draw it again with redraw it. Explain re-. Then use help + -ful in a sentence about a clue that helps.
Check and explain

1: The card is 9 centimetres long; the strip is 3 millimetres wide. 2: Dot and the frog are characters; noon beside the pond gives the setting; losing, finding and placing the feather are plot events. 3: Light feather means not heavy; light to see means illumination. Weighs almost nothing and see help choose. 4: Re- means again in redraw. For example, “The helpful clue showed us where to look.” Helpful describes something that helps.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

Check the earlier word-family examples

“The helpful note showed us the way” means the note helped. “The unhelpful note sent us to the wrong place” means it did not help. “Without a map, the lost toy felt helpless” means unable to help itself in this story. Help is the shared base; -ful, un- and -less change the meaning.

Try a different related word: “The room was tidy. After the game it was ___.” Use un- + tidy. Answer: untidy, meaning not tidy. Check it in the sentence; not every base accepts every affix.

A fresh vocabulary check

Given record: a label is 7 centimetres long. Story: “At night in a tent, Bo lost a torch and found it in a bag.” Report the length, name the setting and a plot event, then explain bright in “The bright torch lit the tent” and “Bo had a bright idea”. Finally replace write again in “Bo will write the label again” with one related word.

Check and explain

The label is 7 centimetres long. The setting is night in a tent. Losing or finding the torch is a plot event. Bright torch gives strong light; bright idea is clever or useful in this context. The surrounding words support the senses. Rewrite means write again: “Bo will rewrite the label.”
